headline: Every format the toolkit detects now renders a report, and a report never prints a private key.
summary: `pki.inspect` rendered four of the fifteen formats `pki.schema.all()` detects, and refused the rest with `inspect/unsupported-format`. It now renders all of them, each through its own named verb as well as through `pki.inspect.any`, so an operator holding a PKCS#12 file or an OCSP response reads it the same way they read a certificate. A PKCS#8 and a PKCS#12 both carry a private key, and neither report prints one: each names the algorithm and says a private key is present, never its bytes.

Added: Ten reports, one per format that had none: `pki.inspect.pkcs8`, `pki.inspect.pkcs12`, `pki.inspect.crmf`, `pki.inspect.cmp`, `pki.inspect.csrattrs`, `pki.inspect.trustanchor`, `pki.inspect.ocspRequest`, `pki.inspect.ocspResponse`, `pki.inspect.tsp` and `pki.inspect.attrcert`. Each takes a PEM string, a DER Buffer, or that format's own parse result, refuses a wrong-format input with its own `inspect/bad-*` code, and is best-effort in the same way the certificate report is: a valid but unusual structure renders rather than throwing.

Every one is reachable by name as well as by detection, and renders the same text either way. A report only `pki.inspect.any` could reach would be a feature nobody could ask for, and an operator who knows what a file is should not have to rely on detection to read it.

No report prints private key material, and for a PKCS#8 key that is structural rather than a check on the private key: the report gives the version, the key algorithm and its parameters, the presence and length of the private key and of a public half, and the type of each attribute, and renders no byte string from inside the file. RFC 5958 has the parser confirm that a version 2 `OneAsymmetricKey` carries a public half and well formed attributes, never that either is unrelated to the private key, so private bytes can sit in the public `BIT STRING` or in any attribute value; a report that wrote either out could be made to write the key out. `pki.key.export` is the verb for the bytes themselves. A PKCS#12 report gives the version, the integrity mode, the MAC algorithm with its iteration count and salt, and one line per safe bag naming its type, nested bags included.

A PKCS#12 report says what reading the contents needs. These verbs take no password, so an encrypted safe is named and not decrypted and the report points at `pki.pkcs12.open`. A report that silently showed nothing would read as an empty store.

`pki.inspect.tsp` renders an RFC 3161 timestamp response: the PKI status with its status strings and failure info, and the TSTInfo inside the token with its policy, message imprint, serial, time, accuracy, ordering, nonce and TSA name. A bare timestamp token is a CMS ContentInfo rather than a response, and `pki.inspect.cms` has always rendered one of those.
Changed: `pki.inspect.any` on an X.509-1997 v1 attribute certificate now throws `attrcert/legacy-v1-not-supported`, the reason that format's own parser gives, where it previously threw `inspect/unsupported-format`. The v1 form is detected so it can be named: RFC 5755 section 1 obsoletes it and this build does not parse it, and a reader of one needs to know which form they hold rather than to go looking for a renderer that was never missing.
The `inspect/unsupported-format` message enumerates the formats that do render, read from the dispatch table rather than from a list written beside it, so it cannot name a set the code does not have.
Fixed: `pki.inspect.cms` on an EnvelopedData, an AuthenticatedData, a CompressedData or a DigestedData now has conformance vectors; before, every CMS report the suite exercised was a SignedData, so the arm reading the other four content types was never driven and a field named wrongly there would have rendered quietly.
